intro: “Jeux de vagues” is the middle movement of La Mer. Woodwind phrases play above plucked strings and quick harp figures, the largest climaxes break up, and the movement ends with a solo flute and a few high string harmonics.

sections.label: A · Wind phrases over harp and pizzicato
sections.mNote: Short wind phrases play above scattered harp and string notes.

sections.label: B · Longer phrases, short exchanges
sections.mNote: The phrases lengthen, then divide into shorter exchanges.

sections.label: C · Winds and strings return
sections.mNote: Quick figures pass through winds and strings towards the crescendo.

sections.label: Coda · Harps, then solo flute
sections.mNote: Harp figures and wind fragments give way to high string harmonics.

cues.title: Woodwind chords over pizzicato strings
cues.text: Soft chords in cor anglais, clarinets and bassoons sound above plucked cellos and basses. Harp figures and short notes on the glockenspiel (celesta is permitted as an alternative) fill the gaps. The violins, divided into several parts, follow in short chords.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, movement II, printed p. 174. The bell part is marked glockenspiel, with celesta permitted as an alternative. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/b/b6/IMSLP15420-Debussy_-_La_Mer_%28orch._score%29.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Tempo marking, Allegro
cues.text: Debussy qualified the Allegro with dans un rythme très souple (in a very supple rhythm). Short accents and triplets shift the phrases across the beat.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, movement II heading, printed p. 174. Cross-rhythms are discussed by Susan Key, https://www.laphil.com/works/la-mer.
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Proofs at Eastbourne, 1905
cues.text: In July 1905 Debussy took the proofs of La Mer to the Grand Hotel in Eastbourne. In a letter from there to his publisher Jacques Durand, he wrote that “the sea unfurls itself with an utterly British correctness”.
cues.evidence: Debussy to Jacques Durand, Eastbourne, summer 1905; the letter and his arrival on 23 July are cited in https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_mer_(Debussy), Background and composition.

cues.title: First performance, Paris, 1905
cues.text: Camille Chevillard conducted the Lamoureux Orchestra in the première of La Mer on 15 October 1905. The Paris audience received it coolly. Three years later, in January 1908, Debussy conducted the work himself in Paris and had an enthusiastic reception.
cues.evidence: Jacob Greenberg’s Boston Symphony programme note gives the 1905 première and Debussy’s Paris performances in January 1908: https://www.bso.org/works/la-mer

cues.title: Short phrase passed between sections
cues.text: A short phrase passes from strings to woodwinds before it has formed a complete tune. Debussy alters its rhythm at each change of instrument. Harps and percussion play brief figures between the orchestral phrases.
cues.evidence: Jacob Greenberg describes the movement’s short melodic cells, rhythmic transformations and exchanges between orchestral sections: https://www.bso.org/works/la-mer. This note concerns the movement’s recurring manner of writing.
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Harp glissandos and clarinet solo
cues.text: The strings play more softly and the wind phrases become shorter. Harp glissandos rise and fall around a clarinet solo marked très doux — very gentle. In the closing pages, instruments drop out one by one.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, printed pp. 218–222, beginning at rehearsal 39: paired harp glissandos, clarinet solo, horns and reduced strings.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Final page, solo flute
cues.text: On the last page a solo flute plays a short phrase above held strings. Six first violins play harmonics, with harp and a few bell notes. The bass stays quiet to the end.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, printed p. 222: flute solo, six first violins in harmonics, harp, glockenspiel and sustained lower strings, mostly ppp.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Harps enter at rehearsal 39
transitions.how: Under En retenant the late crescendo falls away. The double basses sustain and the upper strings stop. At rehearsal 39 the harps play in contrary motion, the horns hold soft notes and a solo clarinet begins a phrase. The bass continues beneath this smaller ensemble.
transitions.evidence: Durand full score, printed pp. 216–218, leading into rehearsal 39. The established coda boundary places the closing retreat.

source.title: Debussy, La Mer · Durand full score, plates D. & F. 6532 / 6838
source.locator: Movement II, printed pp. 174–222: divided and plucked strings at the opening, clarinet and harp glissandos at rehearsal 39, flute and violin harmonics on the last page. The score offers celesta as an alternative to glockenspiel.

timeline.note: Cor anglais, clarinets and bassoons hold soft chords above plucked lower strings; harps and glockenspiel add single notes.
Cor anglais and flute pass short phrases between them while the strings move in quick fragments.
Winds and strings play longer phrases, with harps and percussion sounding across the orchestra.
Harp glissandos surround a quiet clarinet phrase, with held horns and low strings beneath it.
A solo flute plays above harps, glockenspiel and the harmonics of six first violins.

composer.epithet: Composer who trusted his ear over the rules (“pleasure is the law”) and wrote new sounds for the piano, the flute and the orchestra.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1872; piano with Antoine Marmontel, composition with Ernest Guiraud
Prix de Rome 1884 · Paris Exposition 1889 · Pelléas et Mélisande 1902
One completed opera, orchestral triptychs, piano collections, songs, a quartet and three late sonatas
Symbolist poetry · Mussorgsky · the Javanese gamelan · Couperin and Rameau
composer.background:
Debussy was born above his parents’ china shop in Saint-Germain-en-Laye, west of Paris, on 22 August 1862. His parents were not musicians. His father fought for the Paris Commune in 1871 and was imprisoned for it. In prison he met Charles de Sivry, whose mother, Antoinette Mauté, taught the piano and said she had been a pupil of Chopin. She took the boy on as a pupil. In 1872, aged ten, he entered the Paris Conservatoire.

Antoine Marmontel, his piano professor, described him in January 1874 as “a charming child, a truly artistic temperament”; the harmony teacher Émile Durand reported in June 1879 that he was “very gifted in harmony, but hopelessly unfocused”. Around 1890, discussing chords at the piano with his old composition teacher Ernest Guiraud, he said: “There is no theory. You merely have to listen. Pleasure is the law.”
